Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

contents noun

what is in a container, a book or a letter

also content (what is in it), what’s inside, what is in it, table of contents, content and form

classical

Gell. 3.14.3: argentī … quod in eō scyphō inest

quod inest

phrase: a relative clause with īnsum (in with the ablative); plural quae īnsunt

what is in it, the contents

Latin says what is in a thing; it has no general noun for “contents”.

Other words

  • argūmentum, argūmentī n. — the contents of a book, a letter or a play: its subject

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Lewis & Short s.v. argūmentum: “contents, subject, theme”

    Also, and first, a proof or an argument (see subject).

  • rēs, reī f. — the content, as against the words

    noun, fifth declension; opposed to verba · also used · classical · Cic. Or. 51: in philosophiā rēs spectātur, nōn verba penduntur (Lewis & Short)

  • index capitum — table of contents

    phrase: index, indicis m. with the genitive plural of caput · also used · modern · Traupman 389; Traupman 32

    Classically index is a list or catalogue (Quint. 10.1.57) and the title of a book (Lewis & Short); the phrase is Traupman’s. Morgan-Owens gives rērum cōnspectus.

Examples

  • argentī autem, quod in eō scyphō inest, dīmidium meum esse

    but that half of the silver in that cup is mineGell. 3.14.3

  • In amōre haec omnia īnsunt vitia: injūriae, suspīciōnēs, inimīcitiae, indūtiae, bellum, pāx rūrsum.

    in love there are all these faults: wrongs, suspicions, quarrels, truces, war, peace againTer. Eun. 59–61

  • in philosophiā rēs spectātur, nōn verba penduntur

    in philosophy it is the content that counts; words are not weighedCic. Or. 51 (Lewis & Short)

  • Quid inest in hāc arcā?

    What’s in this box?composed

See also subject, container, inside, involve.
